title: ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

reading.body:
This incident illustrates impersonation carried out through AI-generated content, specifically deepfake images and videos used outside any legitimate deployment context. Scammers fabricated a plausible-looking interview article featuring real public figures, a named financial regulator and a known finance journalist, to lend credibility to a fraudulent cryptocurrency platform. The failure is not in a product built by a legitimate AI developer but in the weaponisation of generative AI tools by bad actors to manufacture false authority at scale. The fabricated content was designed to bypass the ordinary social check that familiar faces and polished presentation signal trustworthiness.

The scale reported by ASIC points to a production-line approach: thousands of fake investment platforms and phishing pages removed in a single year, with removal counts roughly doubling or tripling across categories. That volume suggests AI tools lowered the cost of creating convincing fraudulent content enough to make mass deployment practical. There is no indication in the reporting of any platform-level or distribution-level filtering that caught these materials before victims encountered them, which is where automated detection or human review would need to operate to be effective.

What is not established is who is behind any specific campaign, whether any individual has been charged or convicted, and whether the unlicensed platform named in the fabricated article caused financial losses to identifiable victims.

reports.title: The fake Alan Kohler interview that shows a type of scam that’s on the rise
AI deepfake scams 'an emergency in the making' as ASIC reports rise in false investment endorsements
ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

summary:
# Summary

A fake article claiming Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock had a heated confrontation with ABC finance presenter Alan Kohler about an unlicensed cryptocurrency platform called Boulder Sparhaven has highlighted a growing scam problem in Australia. The interview never occurred, but the fabricated story was designed to promote fraudulent investment schemes. According to the Australian Securities and Investments Commission, scammers increasingly use artificial intelligence to create deepfake images and videos of celebrities and politicians to deceive potential investors.

ASIC reports a significant rise in investment fraud, removing 19,400 scams last year, a 182 percent increase. Phishing scams jumped 279 percent with 5,476 removed, while fake investment platforms increased 151 percent with 7,051 taken down. The most commonly impersonated figures include Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, Alan Kohler, and businessman Dick Smith. ASIC advises consumers to verify Australian Financial Services licence numbers independently and warns that polished content and familiar branding do not guarantee legitimacy.
